lessons.title: Collections and Streams
lessons.explanation:
# 03 · Collections and Streams

Every CLI project in this track is, underneath, a collection with a menu
on top: a list of tasks, a map of books by ISBN, a set of tags, a history
of transactions. Picking the right container and knowing which of its
methods *mutate* is most of the job. Streams are the other half: a way to
say "from these, keep those, group by this, sum that" that reads like the
spec.

## The mental model

### 1 · Interfaces in the signature, implementations at `new`

```java
List<String> tasks = new ArrayList<>();          // ordered, indexed
Map<String, Book> byIsbn = new HashMap<>();      // key → value, no order
Set<String> tags = new LinkedHashSet<>();        // unique, insertion order
Deque<Change> history = new ArrayDeque<>();      // stack AND queue
```

The ORDER you get out is a property of the implementation:

| need | List | Set | Map |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| no particular order | `ArrayList` | `HashSet` | `HashMap` |
| insertion order | `ArrayList` | `LinkedHashSet` | `LinkedHashMap` |
| sorted | sort it | `TreeSet` | `TreeMap` |

### 2 · Mutable, unmodifiable, and views

`List.of`, `Set.of`, `Map.of`, `stream().toList()` and `List.copyOf` give
you **unmodifiable** collections — `add` throws. `new ArrayList<>(x)` gives
you a mutable copy. `Collections.unmodifiableList(x)` is a read-only
**view**: it can't be changed through, but it shows later changes to `x`.

### 3 · A stream is a pipeline, not a container

```java
Map<String, Integer> totals = expenses.stream()
    .filter(e -> !e.refunded())
    .collect(groupingBy(Expense::category, TreeMap::new, summingInt(Expense::cents)));
```

Nothing runs until the terminal operation (`collect`, `toList`, `count`,
`forEach`…). A stream is single-use, and it never modifies its source.

### 4 · Comparators compose

```java
Comparator.comparing(Book::year, nullsLast(reverseOrder()))
          .thenComparing(Book::title)
```

## The details that bite

1. **`list.remove(0)` on a `List<Integer>` removes by INDEX.** Use
   `remove(Integer.valueOf(0))` to remove by value.
2. **Removing inside a for-each throws `ConcurrentModificationException`**
   (usually). Use `Iterator.remove()` or `removeIf`.
3. **`retainAll`, `removeAll`, `addAll`, `sort` mutate the receiver.**
   Copy first if the collection was handed to you.
4. **`Collectors.toMap` throws on duplicate keys** unless you pass a merge
   function.
5. **`groupingBy` on a boolean can lose a key; `partitioningBy` never does.**
6. **`"x".split(regex)` with a leading delimiter yields a leading `""`**;
   `"".split(...)` yields `[""]`.
7. **`Map.get` returns `null` for "missing" AND for "present with null"** —
   `containsKey` tells them apart.
8. **`java.util.Stack` is legacy.** Use `ArrayDeque` via `Deque`.

## Exercises

| # | file | ★ | what you build |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 01 | `01-list-remove.java` | ★☆☆ | remove by id not index; filter as copy vs in place |
| 02 | `02-word-counts.java` | ★☆☆ | word frequencies with merge, TreeMap, top-N |
| 03 | `03-grouping.java` | ★★☆ | a library catalogue grouped, partitioned, merged |
| 04 | `04-comparators.java` | ★★☆ | newest-first with nulls last, case-insensitive titles |
| 05 | `05-expense-pipeline.java` | ★★☆ | an expense report as one stream pipeline |
| 06 | `06-sets.java` | ★☆☆ | tag algebra that doesn't touch its inputs |
| 07 | `07-iterate-and-remove.java` | ★★☆ | returning overdue loans without a CME |
| 08 | `08-undo-stack.java` | ★★★ | undo for a to-do list with an ArrayDeque |

Do the warm-ups and core in order. Stretch if time allows.

---

**Next:** `bootcamp/04-strings-and-time`

javabootcamp/03-collections-and-streams/.instructions:
**Concepts:** List.remove overloads · removeIf · copies vs in-place  
**Level:** ★☆☆ warm-up

A to-do manager stores task ids in a List<Integer> and task lines in a
List<String>. Write removeTask (remove the first task with that ID, not
the task at that position; an unknown id changes nothing), withoutDone
(a NEW list without the lines starting "[x]", input unchanged) and
dropDone (the same filter, but in place on the given list).

    ids = [5, 0, 7];  removeTask(ids, 0)      → ids is [5, 7]
    withoutDone(["[x] milk", "[ ] eggs"])     → ["[ ] eggs"]

hint: List<Integer> has both remove(int index) and remove(Object o).
javabootcamp/03-collections-and-streams/.explanation:
List has two remove methods: remove(int index) and remove(Object o).
With a List<Integer> and an int argument, overload resolution picks
remove(int) — an exact match beats boxing — so `ids.remove(id)` removes
by POSITION. With ids [5, 0, 7], removing task 0 deletes the 5. It even
"works" when id happens to be out of range... by throwing
IndexOutOfBoundsException. Box explicitly: ids.remove(Integer.valueOf
(id)), which removes the first equal element and returns false if
there is none.
withoutDone and dropDone are the same rule with two contracts. A
method that RETURNS a list should not touch its argument: stream +
filter + toList (or copy then removeIf). A method that returns void and
is named like a command is expected to mutate: removeIf(predicate) is
the one-call, iterator-safe way to filter in place.
Naming the contract matters more than the code here. When a reader sees
`var open = withoutDone(tasks);` they assume tasks is unchanged; break
that and you have a bug three files away.

javabootcamp/03-collections-and-streams/.instructions:
**Concepts:** HashMap vs TreeMap · Map.merge · String.split · sorting entries  
**Level:** ★☆☆ warm-up

A quiz engine checks which words its questions overuse. Write
wordCounts: lowercase words (runs of a-z and 0-9) to how often they
appear, as a map whose keys iterate alphabetically. Then write
topWords: the n most frequent words, ties broken alphabetically.

    wordCounts("The cat; the HAT.")      → {cat=1, hat=1, the=2}
    wordCounts("")                       → {}
    topWords("b a b c a b", 2)           → [b, a]

hint: split on a leading delimiter gives you an empty first token.
javabootcamp/03-collections-and-streams/.explanation:
Counting is the canonical map loop, and merge makes it one line:
counts.merge(word, 1, Integer::sum) — insert 1 if absent, otherwise
combine the old value with 1. (The pre-Java-8 version, get / null
check / put, is three lines and one forgotten null away from an NPE.)
The ORDER of a map's keys is a property of the map type: HashMap has
none you can rely on, LinkedHashMap keeps insertion order, TreeMap
sorts keys. "Iterates alphabetically" means TreeMap.
split has a famous edge: "The cat".split("[^a-z0-9]+") is fine, but a
string that STARTS with a delimiter (" hello") yields a leading empty
string, and the empty input "" yields [""] — one empty word. Filter out
empty tokens rather than special-casing each.
topWords sorts the entries with a two-level comparator: count
descending, then word ascending. Map.Entry.comparingByValue(
Comparator.reverseOrder()) is the first level; thenComparing(
Map.Entry.comparingByKey()) the tie-break. Lowercase with Locale.ROOT,
always, for keys.

javabootcamp/03-collections-and-streams/.instructions:
**Concepts:** Collectors.groupingBy · partitioningBy · toMap merge · TreeMap  
**Level:** ★★☆ core

A library tracker builds three summaries of its catalogue (the record
Book is defined above the code you edit):

  titlesByAuthor  author → that author's titles, sorted; authors sorted
  classicSplit    true → how many books are older than the cutoff year,
                  false → how many are not; BOTH keys always present
  newestByAuthor  author → the year of their newest book

    titlesByAuthor([Emma/Austen, Dune/Herbert, Persuasion/Austen])
        → {Austen=[Emma, Persuasion], Herbert=[Dune]}
    classicSplit([], 1950)            → {false=0, true=0}

hint: Collectors.toMap throws on a duplicate key unless you merge.
javabootcamp/03-collections-and-streams/.explanation:
groupingBy(classifier, mapFactory, downstream) is the general form:
classifier picks the key (Book::author), TreeMap::new makes the keys
sorted, and the downstream collector decides what each group becomes —
mapping(Book::title, toList()) turns the group's books into titles.
Sorting the titles happens after collecting; collectingAndThen can do
it inside the collector, or sort each list in a second pass.
partitioningBy is groupingBy for a boolean key, with one extra promise
that the tests check: the result ALWAYS has both true and false, even
for an empty input. groupingBy(b -> b.year() < cutoff) would return {}
for an empty list, and the caller's get(true) would be null.
counting() produces a Long.
toMap(key, value) throws IllegalStateException ("Duplicate key") the
moment two books share an author — which is every real catalogue. The
three-argument form takes a merge function for collisions; Math::max
keeps the newest year. A fourth argument (TreeMap::new) picks the map.

javabootcamp/03-collections-and-streams/.instructions:
**Concepts:** Comparator.comparing · thenComparing · nullsLast · case order  
**Level:** ★★☆ core

A library tracker lists books newest first. Write newestFirst: by year
descending, then by title; books with an unknown (null) year go last;
the input list is left untouched. Then write alphabetical: titles in
case-insensitive order, and for titles equal ignoring case, uppercase
first. The record Book is defined above the code you edit.

    newestFirst([Emma 1815, Dune 1965, Notes null, Ubik 1969])
        → [Ubik 1969, Dune 1965, Emma 1815, Notes null]
    alphabetical(["apple", "Banana", "cherry"]) → [apple, Banana, cherry]
    alphabetical(["b", "B"])                    → [B, b]

hint: Comparator.nullsLast wraps the comparator for the key, not the book.
javabootcamp/03-collections-and-streams/.explanation:
Comparator.comparing(keyExtractor, keyComparator) sorts by a key with a
custom order for that key. The year key needs two adjustments: reverse
order (newest first), and nulls at the end. nullsLast(reverseOrder())
does both: it handles nulls itself and delegates the rest. The classic
wrong turn is comparing(Book::year).reversed() — it throws
NullPointerException the moment it meets a null year, and reversed()
applied to the WHOLE chain would also reverse the tie-break.
thenComparing(Book::title) breaks ties. Each then... only runs when
everything before it said "equal".
Strings' natural order is UTF-16 code-unit order: every uppercase
letter sorts before every lowercase one, so "Banana" < "apple".
String.CASE_INSENSITIVE_ORDER fixes that, and thenComparing(natural)
makes the result deterministic for "b" vs "B" — without it, they
compare equal and keep input order (sort is stable), which a test can
pin down but a reader cannot guess. For human-facing sorting in a real
language, java.text.Collator is the grown-up tool.
Sort a copy: stream().sorted(...).toList(), or new ArrayList<>(books)
then sort.

javabootcamp/03-collections-and-streams/.instructions:
**Concepts:** stream pipelines · filter/map/reduce · summingInt · OptionalInt  
**Level:** ★★☆ core

An expense tracker summarises a month. Refunded expenses never count.
Write totalsByCategory (category → total cents, categories sorted),
topCategories (the n categories with the highest totals, ties by name)
and largest (the biggest single non-refunded expense in cents, 0 when
there is none). The record Expense is defined above the code you edit.

    totalsByCategory([food 500, rent 9000, food 250, food 100 refunded])
        → {food=750, rent=9000}
    topCategories(..., 1)     → [rent]
    largest([])               → 0

hint: mapToInt(...).max() gives an OptionalInt, not an int.
javabootcamp/03-collections-and-streams/.explanation:
A stream pipeline reads like the sentence that specifies it: from the
expenses, keep the ones not refunded, group by category, sum the
cents. Write the filter FIRST so every later step only sees what
counts — a category whose only expense was refunded then never
appears at all, which is what the tests expect.
groupingBy(Expense::category, TreeMap::new, summingInt(Expense::cents))
does grouping, ordering and summing in one collector.
topCategories reuses totalsByCategory (don't re-implement the filter
twice — that is how the two numbers drift apart) and then sorts entries
by value descending, name ascending, limits, and maps to keys.
largest shows the primitive streams: mapToInt avoids boxing and gives
max(), sum(), average() directly. max() returns OptionalInt because an
empty stream HAS no maximum; orElse(0) states the business rule ("no
expenses, largest is zero") explicitly instead of hiding it in a
sentinel like Integer.MIN_VALUE.

javabootcamp/03-collections-and-streams/.instructions:
**Concepts:** HashSet · LinkedHashSet · retainAll · set algebra  
**Level:** ★☆☆ warm-up

A library tracker tags books. Write commonTags (tags on both books),
onlyInOne (tags on exactly one of the two) and uniqueInOrder (a list
with duplicates removed, keeping the FIRST time each item appeared).
The input collections must not change.

    commonTags({java, cli}, {cli, web})          → {cli}
    onlyInOne({java, cli}, {cli, web})           → {java, web}
    uniqueInOrder([b, a, b, c, a])               → [b, a, c]

hint: retainAll and removeAll mutate the set you call them on.
javabootcamp/03-collections-and-streams/.explanation:
Sets do the algebra for you — retainAll is intersection, addAll is
union, removeAll is difference — but every one of them MUTATES the set
it is called on. `a.retainAll(b); return a;` returns the right answer
and quietly deletes tags from the caller's book. Copy first:
`var both = new HashSet<>(a); both.retainAll(b);`.
onlyInOne (the symmetric difference) is union minus intersection, or
(a - b) + (b - a). Both are two copies and a couple of bulk calls.
uniqueInOrder is the LinkedHashSet trick: a set that remembers
insertion order, so `new ArrayList<>(new LinkedHashSet<>(items))`
dedupes and keeps first-seen order in one line. A plain HashSet would
dedupe and scramble; a TreeSet would dedupe and sort — neither is what
was asked. stream().distinct() is the stream spelling of the same
thing (it also keeps encounter order).
Set membership uses equals and hashCode, which is why records and
Strings work as set elements out of the box — and why a class that
overrides only equals breaks them (module 05).

javabootcamp/03-collections-and-streams/.instructions:
**Concepts:** Iterator.remove · fail-fast iterators · Map.replaceAll  
**Level:** ★★☆ core

A library tracker closes the day. Write returnOverdue: remove from the
(mutable) list every loan whose dueDay is before today, and return the
removed loans in their original order; a loan due today is not overdue.
Then write renewAll: push every due day in the map later by `days`, in
place. The record Loan is defined above the code you edit.

    loans = [L1 due 3, L2 due 9, L3 due 4];  returnOverdue(loans, 5)
        → returns [L1, L3], loans is now [L2]
    renewAll({A=3, B=10}, 7)  → the map is now {A=10, B=17}

hint: a for-each loop cannot survive list.remove(...) inside it.
javabootcamp/03-collections-and-streams/.explanation:
`for (var loan : loans) if (...) loans.remove(loan);` compiles and
then throws ConcurrentModificationException — usually. The for-each
loop runs an Iterator, and ArrayList's iterator is fail-fast: any
structural change made behind its back is detected on the next call.
(Sometimes it doesn't throw — removing the second-to-last element ends
the loop early instead, silently skipping the last item. Fail-fast is
best-effort, which is worse than always failing.)
The tools that work: an explicit Iterator and it.remove() (the one
removal the iterator knows about), or removeIf when you don't need the
removed items. Here we need them, so the explicit iterator it is:
collect into `returned`, then it.remove().
Map values can be changed in place without touching the key set:
replaceAll((key, value) -> value + days) rewrites every value in one
pass. Calling put for an EXISTING key while iterating entrySet is
allowed too (it is not a structural change), but replaceAll says it
better. Adding or removing keys mid-iteration is what throws.

javabootcamp/03-collections-and-streams/.instructions:
**Concepts:** ArrayDeque as a stack · command history · unmodifiable views  
**Level:** ★★★ stretch

A to-do manager gets an undo key. Finish the nested class TodoList:
add appends a task; remove deletes the first matching task and returns
whether it found one; undo reverts the most recent add or SUCCESSFUL
remove (a removed task returns to the position it had) and returns
false when there is nothing to undo; tasks returns a read-only view.

    add("milk"); add("eggs"); remove("milk");   tasks → [eggs]
    undo()                                      tasks → [milk, eggs]
    undo()                                      tasks → [milk]

hint: remember what to reverse, not what the list looked like.
javabootcamp/03-collections-and-streams/.explanation:
Undo is a stack: the last change is the first one reverted. In Java,
the stack you want is ArrayDeque used through the Deque interface —
push, pop, isEmpty. The old java.util.Stack class is synchronized,
extends Vector, and is kept only for compatibility.
What goes on the stack? Not snapshots of the whole list (that costs
O(n) per change) but a small record of the inverse: "remove the task at
index i" for an add, "insert this task at index i" for a remove. Here
that is a record Change(boolean wasAdd, int index, String task); a
Deque<Runnable> of ready-made inverse actions works just as well.
The position matters: undoing a remove must put the task back where it
was, not at the end, so remove records indexOf BEFORE removing.
A remove that found nothing changed nothing, so it must not push a
history entry — otherwise the next undo "reverts" a no-op and the user
has to press undo twice.
tasks() returns Collections.unmodifiableList(tasks): a read-only VIEW
that reflects later changes, and throws UnsupportedOperationException
on add. Handing out the real list would let callers bypass the history.
